analysis.one_liner: Requires stronger rear, side, and front underride guards on large trucks and trailers.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill requiring underride guards on large trucks, with 17 Senate cosponsors including the leading Republican, died in the Senate Commerce Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a car hits the side or rear of a large truck, it can slide underneath, shearing off the roof and killing or maiming the people inside. This bill would require trucks and trailers to carry strong guards at the rear, sides, and front that stop a car from sliding under, tested to hold up at 35 miles per hour. It also requires drivers to inspect the guards for rust, cracks, and loose bolts, creates a federal committee to oversee the rules, and orders the Transportation Department to publish data on underride crash victims.
analysis.who_benefits: Passenger-vehicle occupants: hundreds of people die each year in underride crashes, and NHTSA and the NTSB have both found many are preventable with better guards. Crash victims' families pushed for the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Requires DOT to issue final rules within a year mandating rear and side underride guards on trailers and single unit trucks over 10,000 pounds, and front guards on semi-trucks, with a performance standard that guards must prevent the truck's body or frame from intruding into a car's passenger compartment at 35 mph, verified by crash tests at full, 50%, and 30% overlap.

Requires drivers to inspect the underride protection system before trips for rust-perforated metal, cracked welds, cracked vertical members, cuts and tears, and missing or loose fasteners, and to complete repairs before operating the vehicle.

Creates a Committee on Underride Protection that includes crash-victim family members, safety engineers, and consumer groups to monitor the rulemaking, and orders DOT to publish quarterly-updated data on underride crash victims on a public website.
Orders research into high-capacity rear barrier prototypes effective at speeds up to 65 mph and periodic reviews to upgrade the standards as technology improves.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies, trailer manufacturers, and truck makers would pay for the new equipment and inspections, and added side-guard weight can slightly reduce how much cargo a trailer can carry, costs that would partly reach consumers through shipping prices.

drawbacks.text: The mandate imposes real equipment and inspection costs on motor carriers and trailer manufacturers, and side guards add weight that can reduce payload capacity, so the requirement would raise operating costs and partly show up in shipping prices.
Compliance is required only for newly manufactured trucks and trailers, so the safety benefits arrive gradually as the existing fleet turns over rather than immediately.

Some in the trucking industry have argued that side guards add weight and cost without proportional safety benefit, a position reflected in the industry's lack of support for the bill; the bill's answer is the crash-test performance standard itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The human stakes are large and the fixes are well understood: federal safety agencies have recommended stronger guards for years, and the bill sets a concrete crash-test standard rather than vague rules. The costs fall on a specific industry in the form of equipment and lost payload, which would partly pass to consumers through shipping prices, but the bill phases compliance in over years for new vehicles only. On balance, the safety gain for ordinary drivers outweighs the equipment costs; the bill's real weakness is that it never got a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2021, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and sat there with no markup, hearing, or floor vote until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the bill on March 4, 2021 with 12 original cosponsors, including Sen. Marco Rubio, a leading Republican, making the sponsorship bipartisan from the start.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action on it.
It ended the Congress with 17 cosponsors: 2 of the 50 Senate Republicans, 14 of the 48 Senate Democrats, and 1 of the 2 Independents, but no committee markup and no floor vote ever occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking companies, trailer manufacturers, and truck makers are better off because the bill died: they avoid the equipment costs and payload losses of mandatory rear, side, and front underride guards, while underride crashes continue at roughly their existing rate.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and built a bipartisan cosponsor list.

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: 17 Senate cosponsors (2 of 50 Republicans, 14 of 48 Democrats, 1 of 2 Independents)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, which then drew no further action from the committee.

for.name: Families of underride crash victims
for.what_they_did: Campaigned publicly for federal underride guard requirements after losing family members in underride crashes; the bill's findings list dozens of victims by name.

against.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or hearing on the bill; it sat without action from referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan: 14 of 48 Democrats, 2 of 50 Republicans, and 1 of 2 Independents cosponsored, led by a Democrat and a prominent Republican, and no committee action or vote ever split along party lines because none occurred.

industries.note: The bill would require carriers to buy and maintain underride guards, run pre-trip inspections, and repair worn guards before operating. Their interest in avoiding the equipment and payload costs runs against the safety of people in passenger vehicles.

Manufacturers would have to redesign and equip trailers and trucks with rear, side, and front guards meeting crash-test standards. Their cost of compliance is the direct flip side of the bill's safety benefit.

The bill would seat an insurance industry representative on the oversight committee, and fewer catastrophic underride fatalities means fewer large injury claims. Its interest in this bill runs alongside public safety.
